summary: This part of the Privacy Enhanced Mail series defines certificate-based key management, an approach where trusted authorities vouch for the encryption keys that belong to people. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1422 describes how Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) users could obtain and check public keys through signed certificates. It proposes a hierarchy of authorities and procedures for checking revoked certificates.

questions: how does privacy enhanced mail manage keys
what is pem certificate based key management
subtitle: The certificate hierarchy proposed for Privacy Enhanced Mail.

tldr.problem: Privacy Enhanced Mail needs public keys that senders and recipients can connect to the named people or organizations.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines certificates and a hierarchy in which the IPRA certifies PCAs, PCAs certify CAs, and CAs certify users; certificate paths and revocation lists support validation.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1422 is marked Historic in the supplied metadata and obsoletes RFC 1114; it is not a current standard.

today: RFC 1422 is marked Historic in the supplied metadata and obsoletes RFC 1114. The metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why PEM Needs Key Management
sections.content:
This memo is Part II of the Privacy Enhanced Mail series. It defines a certificate-based key-management architecture to provide the public keys needed by message senders and recipients.

The design follows the 1988 X.509 authentication framework and adds conventions for a shared certification hierarchy, policy publication and validation. The RFC anticipates use with PEM and says the infrastructure could also support other protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: To encrypt mail for someone or verify their signature, a user needs that person's public key. This memo describes how certificates can connect a key to an identity.

sections.title: Certificates and Mail Processing
sections.content:
A certificate names a subject, provides the subject's public component and identifies the issuer that vouches for their connection. The issuer signs the certificate, which also contains a validity period and other fields.

Before encrypting a message, a sender obtains and validates each recipient's certificate, then uses the public component to encrypt the data-encryption key. For message integrity and origin authentication, a sender signs a message integrity code; recipients validate the certificate and compare the recovered code with a locally calculated one.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate contains a public key and the name it belongs to, together with an issuer's signature. Mail software checks the certificate before relying on the key.

sections.title: The Certification Hierarchy
sections.content:
The Internet Policy Registration Authority (IPRA) is the hierarchy's root. It certifies Policy Certification Authorities (PCAs); each PCA publishes its policy and certifies Certification Authorities (CAs); CAs certify users and subordinate entities.

The memo describes organizational, residential and PERSONA CAs. A PERSONA CA issues certificates that do not claim to validate the user's real identity. The design uses distinguished names and rules intended to limit duplicate names.
sections.plainLanguage: The hierarchy begins with one registration authority, followed by policy authorities, certification authorities and users. An anonymous-use certificate does not claim that its name identifies the user's real identity.

sections.title: Revoking and Validating Certificates
sections.content:
A CA can revoke a certificate if a private component may be compromised or a user's affiliation changes. Revocations appear on a Certificate Revocation List (CRL); the format includes both the issue date and the next scheduled issue date so users can identify stale lists.

Validation checks certificate signatures up the chain to the IPRA, checks validity periods, and checks current CRLs. Software must at least warn users about expired or revoked certificates and unavailable or outdated CRLs; local policy may reject them.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificate checks follow issuer signatures to the root authority and confirm that each certificate is current. They also check lists of certificates that have been cancelled.

sections.title: Protecting Private Components
sections.content:
The memo says users must protect their private components because PEM's security depends on their secrecy. It recommends generating key pairs with unpredictable randomness and gives a date-and-time-only random seed as a poor example.

A certification authority's private component also needs strong protection because certificates signed with it depend on that authority's guarantee. The memo states that no CA needs access to a user's private component.
sections.plainLanguage: A user's private key must remain secret, and its generation needs unpredictable input. A CA must also protect its signing key because certificates depend on it.
